paragraphs: The paper addresses how to identify individual neural spikes in extracellular voltage recordings. Clustering methods can require substantial human supervision and make systematic mistakes when spikes overlap in time. The authors instead describe the recording as a noisy combination of signals from several neurons, with each neuron contributing its own spike waveform.

Their method jointly estimates those waveforms and the sparse sequences of spike events that produced the recording. This is blind deconvolution because both the underlying events and their associated waveforms must be inferred. They formulate the estimation using maximum a posteriori inference and develop a block-coordinate descent algorithm to approximate the solution.

The authors evaluate the method on simulated recordings and real recordings with ground truth supplied by simultaneous intracellular measurements. In both settings, it substantially reduces missed spikes and false detections relative to a standard clustering algorithm, mainly by recovering overlapping spikes. These findings support a fully automated alternative that directly accounts for signal overlap instead of treating it as a source of clustering errors.
neurips-2011-a-blind-sparse-deconvolutio.tldr: Jointly estimating neural spike events and waveforms improves recovery of overlapping spikes compared with a standard clustering method.

paragraphs: Approximate reinforcement learning methods can repeatedly change their policies without settling down, a behavior called policy oscillation. The paper revisits this problem by connecting two families of methods: fast greedy updates based on estimated value functions, and value-based policy gradient methods. It shows that a considerable subset of the former can be viewed as a limiting case of the latter.

This connection provides an explanation for oscillation, which the authors illustrate with artificial examples. It also leads to a constrained natural actor-critic algorithm that can interpolate between the two approaches. The contribution therefore includes both a way to understand unstable policy updates and an algorithm derived from that understanding.

The paper separately examines the suggestion that oscillation explains the poor performance of approximate dynamic programming on Tetris. Its empirical evidence argues against that connection and supports an alternative explanation. It also reports improved Tetris scores relative to existing dynamic programming results. The evidence distinguishes understanding oscillation from establishing the cause of poor benchmark performance.
neurips-2011-a-reinterpretation-of-the-p.tldr: A connection between greedy value methods and policy gradients explains policy oscillation and motivates an algorithm that bridges the two approaches.

paragraphs: Learning from several related datasets becomes difficult when the target data follow a different distribution and have few or no labels. Differences can concern both which inputs occur and how labels relate to those inputs. The paper addresses both forms of mismatch, rather than relying on the assumption that input-label relationships remain similar across domains.

The proposed framework combines source data with target data through two stages of weighting. First, it estimates weights independently to reduce differences in marginal distributions. Second, it computes weights jointly to address differences in conditional distributions. Joint computation in the second stage allows the method to exploit possible interactions among the available sources.

The authors analyze generalization using weighted Rademacher complexity, connecting the weighting formulation to its ability to perform beyond the training data. Comparisons with existing domain adaptation methods on three real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The central contribution is a framework that treats both kinds of distribution shift explicitly while coordinating how multiple sources contribute to learning.
neurips-2011-a-two-stage-weighting-frame.tldr: Two-stage weighting adapts multiple source datasets by addressing both input-distribution differences and changes in input-label relationships.

paragraphs: Knowledge-based support vector machines use expert advice alongside training examples. That advice can improve generalization, but imperfect advice can also lead to worse models. The paper addresses this weakness by allowing the learning process to revise the advice itself, so expert knowledge becomes something the model can improve while learning from data.

The proposed extension jointly learns a predictive model and refines the supplied advice. This is particularly relevant when labeled examples are scarce, a setting where the authors describe the method as effective for knowledge discovery. Its output can therefore be useful in two ways: as a learned predictor and as an improved version of the original expert guidance.

The formulation includes bilinear constraints, and the authors solve it with two iterative strategies: successive linear programming and a constrained concave-convex approach. Experiments show useful refinements to expert advice together with improved learning performance. These results support treating advice as revisable information, rather than assuming that all supplied knowledge is already accurate enough to guide the model unchanged.
neurips-2011-advice-refinement-in-knowle.tldr: An extension of knowledge-based SVMs jointly improves expert advice and learns a predictor, with experiments showing benefits for both.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a reinforcement learning agent can combine learning from a teacher with learning through its own exploration. Its starting point is an apprenticeship learning framework that uses teacher demonstrations but does not necessarily explore the environment. The authors modify that framework so the student can use both sources of experience.

One change replaces the previous Mistake Bound model learners with a framework combining the KWIK and Mistake Bound supervised learning protocols. A second change adds communication of expected utility from the student to the teacher. Together, these changes make the student's own learning situation relevant to how teaching is used, rather than relying solely on demonstration traces.

The resulting system uses teacher traces only when the agent needs concepts that it cannot learn efficiently by itself. The authors present theoretical and empirical results for this combined framework. Its significance is the selective role assigned to teaching: demonstrations support concepts that are difficult for autonomous learning, while exploration remains part of the student's overall learning process.
neurips-2011-blending-autonomous-explora.tldr: A combined apprenticeship and reinforcement learning framework uses teacher traces when the student cannot efficiently learn the needed concepts alone.

paragraphs: Skill discovery in reinforcement learning often starts by identifying useful subgoal states or regions. However, several different subgoals may represent the same underlying skill. Treating every subgoal separately can create an inefficient collection of skills, while tying each skill to a particular state space can restrict its reuse across tasks.

The paper proposes clustering subgoal data expressed in an agent-space. Instead of making each discovered subgoal its own skill goal, the method uses the resulting clusters as templates for skill termination conditions. These conditions specify when a skill has achieved its purpose, allowing corresponding subgoals to be represented through a shared template.

A Dirichlet process mixture model supplies the clustering mechanism used to discover a minimal, sufficient collection of portable skills. This addresses the question of how many distinct skills are appropriate alongside the question of which subgoals matter. The contribution is a way to consolidate redundant subgoals and support transfer without requiring every task to have an identical state space.
neurips-2011-clustering-via-dirichlet-pr.tldr: Clustering subgoals in an agent-space produces shared skill termination templates and a minimal, sufficient collection of portable skills.

paragraphs: The paper considers decisions with a distinct period for experimentation followed by a period of commitment. During experimentation, the decision maker can try different options. Once commitment begins, one option must be chosen and retained. Both phases incur costs, but experimentation is more expensive, making the duration of exploration part of the decision problem.

The authors analyze regret in this two-phase bandit setting and propose algorithms with upper and lower bounds. These bounds depend on the ratio between the lengths of the experimentation and commitment phases. This dependence captures why the value of gathering more information must be considered together with how long the eventual choice will remain in effect.

When the decision maker can choose the phase lengths, the analysis finds that the optimal experimentation duration scales logarithmically with the total time horizon. Thus, a longer horizon calls for more experimentation, but the optimal number of exploratory steps grows much more slowly than the horizon itself. This conclusion applies to the paper's setup, including its higher experimentation costs and subsequent fixed commitment.
neurips-2011-committing-bandits-c12aafaf.tldr: In a bandit model with costly experimentation followed by fixed commitment, the optimal experimentation duration grows logarithmically with the time horizon.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a temporal restricted Boltzmann machine for modeling an output sequence conditional on an input sequence. This makes the relationship between two sequences the central modeling task. The model describes possible outputs in relation to a supplied input, while also representing the temporal structure involved in how those outputs develop.

The authors emphasize several properties inherited from restricted Boltzmann machines: efficient exact inference, the ability to capture nonlinear structure and dynamics, and an exponentially more expressive latent state than that of hidden Markov models. These properties combine computational tractability for inference with a rich internal representation of sequence behavior and input-output relationships.

The application is facial expression transfer, presented as a challenging graphics problem involving high-dimensional data. Experiments cover both two-dimensional and three-dimensional data and show improved performance over several baselines. The findings support this conditional temporal model for the tested transfer task, connecting its sequence-modeling capabilities to a concrete application where nonlinear structure and dynamics both need to be represented.
neurips-2011-facial-expression-transfer-.tldr: A conditional temporal restricted Boltzmann machine models nonlinear sequence relationships and improves facial expression transfer over several tested baselines.

paragraphs: Latent tree models represent hierarchical and long-range relationships through a tree containing hidden variables. Such relationships arise in vision, bioinformatics, and language problems. The paper addresses two restrictions of existing approaches: computational pressure toward discrete or Gaussian variables, and reliance on heuristic local search when estimating tree structure and model parameters.

The authors propose representing distributions through kernel embeddings. This allows their latent tree method to handle continuous variables whose distributions need not be Gaussian. The approach covers several parts of the modeling process, including recovering the hidden tree structure, learning parameters, and carrying out inference once the model has been learned.

The paper provides provable guarantees for structure recovery and describes parameter learning that avoids local minima, together with efficient inference. Experiments on simulated and real data show advantages for the proposed approach. The contribution therefore combines broader distributional modeling with a different learning strategy, addressing both what latent trees can represent and how their structure and parameters can be estimated.
neurips-2011-kernel-embeddings-of-latent.tldr: Kernel embeddings enable latent tree models with continuous, non-Gaussian variables, guaranteed structure recovery, and parameter learning free of local minima.

paragraphs: Recognizing images across thousands of categories raises challenges beyond those encountered in medium-sized datasets. Large structured datasets also supply useful information: categories can be connected through a semantic hierarchy. The paper investigates how these conceptual relationships can guide image categorization, so the learning process makes explicit use of relationships among object classes.

The proposed method uses the category hierarchy in two ways. It helps define the loss function that guides learning, and it guides the selection of shared features for related categories. Semantic structure therefore influences both how predictions are evaluated during training and which visual information related categories use in common.

To make the approach practical at scale, the authors introduce an optimization method combining proximal approximation with accelerated parallel gradient computation. They evaluate it on an ImageNet subset containing 1.2 million images from 1,000 categories. The reported results demonstrate effectiveness and promise in that setting, supporting category relationships as useful information for large-scale recognition alongside the image features themselves.
neurips-2011-large-scale-category-struct.tldr: Using category hierarchies to shape losses and share features shows promise for image categorization across 1,000 ImageNet categories.

paragraphs: Many networks provide both connections between nodes and descriptive features for each node. The paper asks how those features can be compared in a way that reflects the network's connections. Its structure preserving metric learning method, SPML, learns a Mahalanobis distance metric tied to the connectivity already present in the network.

Structure preservation has a specific meaning here: applying a connectivity rule, such as nearest neighbors, using the learned distances yields the correct connections. The learning objective therefore links feature-based distance to network construction. This makes the distance function useful for understanding how node attributes relate to observed links and for predicting link patterns from those attributes.

Synthetic and real-world experiments show more accurate link-pattern prediction than standard techniques. The authors also develop a stochastic gradient descent optimization method that they describe as removing the running-time dependency on network size, enabling applications with thousands of nodes and millions of edges. The contribution pairs a connectivity-aware metric with an optimization approach intended to make that metric practical for large networks.
neurips-2011-learning-a-distance-metric-.tldr: SPML learns distances between node features that preserve network connectivity and improve link-pattern prediction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Loopy belief propagation approximates probabilities in graphical models containing loops. A natural response to its errors is to adjust the model parameters until its answers match desired marginal probabilities. The paper shows that this strategy has a fundamental obstacle: many target marginals cannot be reached by belief propagation, regardless of the parameters or learning algorithm used.

The authors call these targets unbelievable marginals. They identify a condition under which this problem occurs: the Hessian of the Bethe free energy at the target is not positive-definite. In those cases, learning cannot make belief propagation attain the target, and the resulting beliefs may even be worse than the approximation obtained before learning.

The paper also demonstrates a way to reach such targets through averaging. Belief propagation is run using parameters perturbed around learned mean values, and the resulting inaccurate beliefs are combined. Their average can achieve marginals that an individual run cannot. This distinguishes the limitations of learning a single parameter setting from the possibilities created by aggregating several approximate outputs.
neurips-2011-learning-unbelievable-proba.tldr: Some marginal probabilities are unreachable by belief propagation under any parameter setting, but averaging beliefs from perturbed models can achieve them.

paragraphs: The Precis problem asks for a fixed number of data points that summarize a large dataset while remaining diverse. Representativeness and diversity serve different purposes: the selection should reflect the dataset without spending its limited size on redundant examples. The paper considers this problem for applications including video and document summarization, exploration, and pre-filtering.

The authors develop a formulation covering both ordinary vector spaces and non-Euclidean manifolds. They introduce measures of selection quality that use the manifold's own geometry to assess representativeness and diversity. This extends the selection problem to data such as shapes, human activities, and textures, where the relevant geometry may differ from ordinary vector-space distance.

An annealing-based iterative alternation algorithm optimizes the resulting cost function. The formulation can use known manifold geometry or geometry estimated from samples, making it applicable under both circumstances. Experimental results support its strength and generality. The central contribution is a common framework for selecting compact, varied summaries while taking the geometry of the data into account.
neurips-2011-manifold-precis-an-annealin.tldr: A geometry-aware selection framework uses annealing to choose representative, diverse subsets from vector spaces and non-Euclidean manifolds.

paragraphs: Maximum covariance unfolding addresses dimensionality reduction when observations come from two naturally aligned sources. It constructs a common low-dimensional representation that strengthens correlations across the sources while preserving local distances within each one. The objective thus combines shared information between modalities with the neighborhood structure specific to each modality.

The paper explores two applications. For paired EEG and fMRI data, it seeks to visualize which fMRI voxels are most strongly associated with changes in EEG traces. An additional metric-learning step in the original voxel space supports this visualization. The second application retrieves corresponding image and text samples from Wikipedia across the two modalities.

The authors also develop a faster implementation for larger problems using ideas from spectral graph theory. This transforms the original semidefinite programming formulation into a simpler semidefinite quadratic linear programming problem. The work therefore combines a joint representation objective, applications that use cross-modal relationships, and a computational reformulation intended to make the approach manageable at larger scales.
neurips-2011-maximum-covariance-unfoldin.tldr: Maximum covariance unfolding jointly embeds two aligned modalities while maximizing cross-modal correlations and preserving local distances within each source.

paragraphs: Filtering estimates a changing state from measurements, but outliers can make that estimation unreliable. This paper assumes that the posterior density would have a single mode without the unwanted outliers. Under that assumption, it seeks a point estimate directly, avoiding both an explicit model of the outliers and a general approximation of the whole posterior.

The approach combines finite-dimensional filtering, such as an Extended Kalman Filter or Unscented Filter, with semi-supervised multiple instance learning. It begins with a candidate set of inlier measurements. State estimation and inlier identification are then treated as linked regression and classification problems, allowing the method to update both its state estimate and its judgment of which measurements belong.

The authors show that these updates can proceed iteratively and causally using only the current measurement. They illustrate the method through visual tracking with occlusions and deformations, starting from partial target information supplied as a bounding box. The contribution is a filtering procedure that jointly tracks the target and revises the measurements considered reliable.
neurips-2011-multiple-instance-filtering.tldr: Multiple instance filtering jointly estimates a changing state and its inlier measurements under a unimodality assumption for the outlier-free posterior.

paragraphs: The paper investigates when spectral clustering can recover clusters exactly despite noise in the similarities between data points. Its hierarchical analysis focuses on a class of similarity matrices with hierarchical structure. For that class, the studied algorithm can recover the entire cluster hierarchy with high probability even when the permitted noise grows with the number of points.

The authors also strengthen previous results for partitioning data into a fixed number of clusters. They derive conditions under which spectral clustering makes no assignment mistakes. These are conditional recovery statements: their significance lies in identifying settings where a commonly used method can be given an exact-recovery guarantee.

A minimax analysis provides tight upper and lower bounds for the clustering problem, establishing information-theoretic reference points against which spectral clustering can be compared. This separates questions about the particular algorithm from questions about what the available information permits. Experiments with simulated and real-world data illustrate the theoretical results, connecting the noise analysis to observed clustering behavior.
neurips-2011-noise-thresholds-for-spectr.tldr: The paper establishes noise conditions for exact spectral clustering recovery and compares its performance with information-theoretic limits.

paragraphs: The paper studies causal models that allow feedback loops. Each variable is described as a potentially nonlinear function of its parent variables plus additive noise. The central question is whether the causal connections can be learned from observations even when influences form cycles, rather than following a one-way ordering through the variables.

The authors prove generic identifiability of the causal graph for the two-variable case with Gaussian noise. Generic identifiability means the result concerns the general case within that setting, rather than guaranteeing recovery for every possible model. The stated scope matters: the theorem is specifically about bivariate models with the given noise assumption.

They also propose a method for learning these models from observational data. Without cycles, it reduces to ordinary regression. With cycles, an additional loss term appears, connecting the problem to nonlinear independent component analysis. Synthetic data illustrate the method. Together, these contributions show how feedback changes both the theoretical recovery question and the objective used to learn the model.
neurips-2011-on-causal-discovery-with-cy.tldr: Cyclic additive-noise models are generically identifiable in the bivariate Gaussian-noise case, and a proposed learning method accounts explicitly for feedback.

paragraphs: The paper is motivated by selecting a representative subset of training data and by the poor practical performance of the minimum norm algorithm in that application. The authors report running time around O(n^7), including O(n^5) oracle calls. This motivates a faster approach to minimizing submodular functions, with approximation available when exact optimization is not supplied by their method.

The proposed algorithm can be applied to arbitrary submodular functions and is exact for a large subclass. For other functions, it repeatedly constructs tight submodular upper bounds and optimizes them. The process replaces the original objective with successive bounding objectives, providing an iterative route to an approximate solution.

The authors establish theoretical properties and report empirical results suggesting substantial speedups over minimum norm while retaining higher accuracies. The exactness claim remains specific to the stated subclass; the broader method is approximate. Its contribution is a practical alternative motivated by a concrete data-selection bottleneck, with both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence supporting the proposed optimization strategy.
neurips-2011-on-fast-approximate-submodu.tldr: An iterative upper-bound method offers fast approximate submodular minimization and is exact for a large subclass of objectives.

paragraphs: Comparing probability distributions is useful for tasks such as outlier detection, transfer learning, and testing whether two samples come from the same distribution. One approach estimates a density ratio directly instead of estimating both densities separately. However, ordinary density ratios can fluctuate strongly, making the resulting divergence estimates difficult to obtain reliably.

The paper proposes using relative divergences, which require estimating relative density ratios. The authors show that these ratios are smoother than their ordinary counterparts, giving the method favorable nonparametric convergence behavior. The key change is therefore in the quantity being estimated: a smoother comparison can be easier to learn from samples.

Under a parametric setup, the proposed divergence estimator also has asymptotic variance independent of model complexity. The authors interpret this as indicating little overfitting even with complex models. That conclusion is tied to the stated asymptotic analysis, rather than an unconditional finite-sample guarantee. Experiments demonstrate the approach's usefulness, complementing the theoretical reasons for choosing relative distribution comparisons.
neurips-2011-relative-density-ratio-esti.tldr: Relative density ratios yield smoother distribution comparisons, favorable convergence behavior, and model-complexity-independent asymptotic variance in a parametric setting.

paragraphs: The paper studies short-term financial trend prediction when a model is allowed to abstain. The objective is to improve accuracy on the predictions it chooses to make, accepting that some cases will receive no prediction. This introduces a trade-off between coverage, meaning how often the model predicts, and accuracy on those selected cases.

The authors examine two selection mechanisms for hidden Markov model predictors. The first rejects predictions according to an ambiguity principle. The second identifies low-quality hidden states and avoids predicting when the model is in those states. This second approach, called a selective HMM, uses the model's internal state structure to guide abstention.

Both mechanisms allow coverage to be traded for accuracy in a controlled way. The reported comparison finds both effective and favors the selective HMM approach. The findings concern selective prediction performance: the benefit comes from making predictions on a chosen subset of cases. They support using state-level quality information as a useful basis for deciding when an HMM should predict.
neurips-2011-selective-prediction-of-fin.tldr: Allowing HMMs to abstain improves financial trend prediction accuracy at reduced coverage, with state-based selection performing best in the reported comparison.

paragraphs: Non-negative least squares is a simple regression approach for settings involving non-negative quantities. Its practical usefulness can seem doubtful in high-dimensional linear models, where overfitting is a concern. The paper investigates whether this basic method can still recover sparse solutions, meaning solutions in which only a limited set of coefficients contribute.

The authors show that, for a broad class of designs, non-negative least squares resists overfitting and works well for sparse recovery when combined with thresholding. Thresholding removes coefficients that do not pass the chosen cutoff. The result therefore concerns the combination of a non-negativity-constrained fit and a subsequent selection step, within the stated class of designs.

In experiments, the approach even outperforms L1 regularization. Non-negative least squares also avoids the delicate choice of a regularization parameter, which motivates the authors' suggestion that it may be a preferred method. The findings challenge the expectation that high-dimensional recovery necessarily requires that form of regularization, while keeping the theoretical design conditions and empirical nature of the comparison explicit.
neurips-2011-sparse-recovery-by-threshol.tldr: For a broad class of designs, non-negative least squares combined with thresholding supports sparse recovery and outperforms L1 regularization in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper combines three hypotheses about classification: the distribution of inputs contains useful information about labels, data concentrate near low-dimensional manifolds, and different classes occupy separate manifolds divided by low-density regions. Together, these assumptions suggest that learning the shape of the input distribution can help determine which local changes should leave a prediction stable.

High-order contractive auto-encoders learn that local geometry. The authors describe the representation as an atlas of local charts, with each chart characterized by principal singular vectors of the representation mapping's Jacobian. In plain language, these vectors identify local directions associated with the learned manifold. The representation learners can also be stacked into a deep architecture.

A version of TangentProp then encourages the classifier to remain insensitive to changes along those learned directions, without requiring domain-specific knowledge to supply them. The authors report record-breaking classification results. The contribution links unsupervised geometry learning to supervised prediction through an explicit invariance objective, using learned local structure to guide how the classifier responds to nearby inputs.
neurips-2011-the-manifold-tangent-classi.tldr: The manifold tangent classifier learns local manifold directions and encourages prediction stability along them, reporting record-breaking classification results.

paragraphs: Scene understanding often requires context from other image regions as well as local features. However, the relevance of that context can depend on where a region lies in the image. Giving every location its own contextual parameters captures this variation but creates a very large model, especially when several scene-understanding tasks are considered.

The paper addresses this parameter growth by placing a Markov random field over the parameters themselves. Parameter sets are encouraged to resemble one another when their locations are spatially close or their tasks are semantically close. This encodes structure in how the predictors are parameterized, allowing spatial and semantic relationships to guide their learning.

The authors explain that the method is, in principle, complementary to approaches that place graphical models over output labels. Evaluations cover object detection, scene categorization, depth estimation, and geometric labeling, with reported improvements over state-of-the-art methods in all four tasks. These findings support structured relationships among parameters as a useful way to incorporate context across locations and tasks.
neurips-2011-theta-mrf-capturing-spatial.tldr: An MRF over model parameters encourages spatially and semantically related predictors to share structure, improving four scene-understanding tasks in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Large object-detection datasets can still contain classes with very few training examples. The paper addresses this uneven supply of data by allowing a target class to use examples from other classes. The goal is to expand the training material available for a class whose own examples are insufficient, drawing on information already present elsewhere in the dataset.

The model learns both which outside examples to borrow and how to transform them to resemble examples of the target class more closely. Selection and transformation are therefore both part of the learning problem. This makes the contribution more specific than simply pooling data across classes: the borrowed instances are chosen and adapted for the class receiving them.

Experiments on the SUN09 object-detection dataset show that the resulting detector improves on the state-of-the-art detector used in the comparison. The findings support cross-class example borrowing as a way to strengthen object detection when some classes are poorly represented. The reported benefit comes from training with examples that are both borrowed and transformed.
neurips-2011-transfer-learning-by-borrow.tldr: Learning which examples to borrow from other classes and how to transform them improves object detection on SUN09.

paragraphs: Monte-Carlo Tree Search plans by using simulated outcomes to estimate the value of decisions. Because those simulations are stochastic, their estimates contain both bias and variance. The paper focuses on variance, which concerns fluctuations in the estimates, rather than the bias-reduction approaches that had received more attention through the addition of domain knowledge.

The authors investigate three established statistical techniques: common random numbers, antithetic variates, and control variates. Their contribution is to show how these methods can be applied within Monte-Carlo Tree Search. This connects tools from statistical simulation with a planning procedure whose decisions depend on values estimated from random simulations.

The empirical investigation covers Pig, Can't Stop, and Dominion in stochastic single-agent settings. These experiments explore the techniques' efficacy in the studied planning problems; the abstract does not assert a uniform improvement from every technique. The broader significance is to make variance reduction an explicit part of MCTS design, alongside efforts to improve the bias of its estimates.
neurips-2011-variance-reduction-in-monte.tldr: The paper adapts three classical variance-reduction techniques to Monte-Carlo Tree Search and studies their efficacy in three stochastic single-agent games.
